title: Rabbi Idi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Hyman says that he was a Babylonian and went up to the Land of Israel in the time of R. Ami. See Bava Metzia ch. 5 halakha 2, where R. Idi said: 'When I came up from the exile (to the Land of Israel), I found a case before R. Ami.' In Babylonia it appears to Hyman that he received teaching from Rav Chisda; see Yevamot ch. 11 end of halakha 2: 'R. Idi said before R. Yose (R. Assi), in the name of R. Chisda.'

And Berakhot ch. 1 halakha 2: 'R. Idi and Rav Hamnuna and Rav Ada bar Acha in the name of Rav.' Hyman argues: Without doubt, the plain sense is that R. Idi spoke in the name of Rav Hamnuna, since he received teaching from him while in Babylonia. Likewise, Hyman says that the reading in Tanchuma Lekh Lekha 1, 'R. Idi, R.H., in the name of R. Yose bar R. Yehuda in the name of R. Shmuel,' is a scribal error and should read as in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot ch. 2 halakha 1: 'R. Chuna, R. Uri (it should read R. Idi), Rav Yosef in the name of Rav Yehuda.' So too, Hyman writes, we find R. Idi with R. Huna, both of whom spoke in the name of רשב״נ, in Tanchuma Emor 15. And there, Bereshit 33, 'R.H. said in his name'; Hyman identifies him as the second R. Huna and says that both went up to the Land of Israel.

He is mentioned in Pesachim ch. 9 halakha 1, Sukkah ch. 2 halakha 8, Beitzah ch. 3 halakha 4, Nedarim ch. 6 halakha 8, Sanhedrin ch. 1 halakhot 2-4. Those who spoke in his name: we find Rav Mesharshiya; see Rosh Hashanah ch. 4 halakha 8; and he resolves Rabbi Bun bar Chiyya’s difficulty; see Beitzah ch. 3 halakha 4.
It appears to Hyman that he afterward went down to Babylonia in the time of Rava, and this is what we find in Nedarim 5b, Kiddushin 40a, Bava Metzia 75b: 'Rava said, Rav Idi explained it to me.'

notes.text: The expansion of רשב״נ in the cited Tanchuma Emor15 passage remains unresolved.
The source names Rav Ada bar Acha. Yose/Asi and Uri/Idi are forms Hyman compares or emends; his return-to-Babylonia and second-Huna identifications remain his chronological arguments.

The named Guggenheimer Jerusalem Talmud Bava Metzia 5:2 paragraph explicitly gives Rabbi Idi’s first-person statement that he came up from exile and found a case before Rabbi Ami. Its local full title supports the heading, without proving every chronology or teacher inference in Hyman’s article. The named Beitzah 3:4 paragraph places Rabbi Bun bar Chiyya’s question before Rabbi Idi’s answer; the corrected direction of the difficulty is retained, and Rabbi Bun’s full title has local support. The quoted R.H. abbreviations are left unexpanded; the other source-abbreviated titles retain R. The whole saved Torat Emet Tanchuma Emor 15 scalar does not contain the sought Idi/Huna/רשב״נ chain. That is a bounded edition-and-locator nonmatch, not disproof of another recension or permission to expand רשב״נ. Hyman’s emphatic without-doubt reconstruction, scribal-error assertion, proposed Uri-to-Idi reading, Yose/Asi alternative, second-Huna identification and later return to Babylonia remain attributed at their supplied force. Both existing mixed notes remain verbatim; p002 and all source holds remain. No additional legal material, named people, identity, chronology or teacher graph facts are imported.

The whole printed Rabbi Idi notice in volume I, page 140, was consulted. Subsequent named Guggenheimer readings add important differences: Yevamot 11:2 Hebrew has Idi before Yose in Rav Chisda’s name, while its English first sentence omits the Chisda attribution. Berakhot 1:2 lists Idi, Hamnuna and Ada in Rav’s name and reads the patronymic Ahava beside Hyman’s Acha; this list does not itself establish Hyman’s proposed serial teacher chain. Berakhot 2:1 reads Uri and continues through Rav Yehudah in Shmuel’s name. Its editor reports a Rome-manuscript Ammi alternative; that manuscript has not been independently collated. The consulted Torat Emet Tanchuma Lekh Lekha 1 reads Idi and Huna in Rabbi Yehudah’s name, and Yose in Rabbi Shmuel’s name, unlike the quotation Hyman criticizes. Hyman’s “without doubt,” scribal-error judgment and proposed Uri-to-Idi correction remain explicitly his, rather than repairs to the supplied Hebrew or admissions of personal identity. The cited Bereshit 33 locus and the Emor chain remain unverified in an exact matching recension; a textual error response or bounded nonmatch does not establish absence. רשב״נ remains unexpanded. His second-Huna identification and later return to Babylonia remain attributed chronological arguments.
